leadRef: S&P 500 and Dow enter correction as Nasdaq drops 5.3% and Nvidia sinks 14%
description: The AI sell-off pushes the S&P 500 and Dow into correction and Nvidia falls 14% on an SEC accounting probe; an Anthropic mathematician says Claude helped prove the Riemann Hypothesis; Trump threatens to ban US firms' data centres abroad; Arizona opens a criminal probe into rogue AI agents in banks.

thirtySecond.p: Anthropic's Levent Alpöge says he and Claude proved the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis in a huge Lean file that experts have started checking.
Trump says US companies will not be allowed to build AI data centres overseas and threatens a 'tremendous tax'.
Arizona's attorney general opens a criminal investigation into OpenAI and other AI firms over AI agents getting into bank accounts.

footerNote: Saturday's deep beat, markets, business and world: the AI sell-off became a correction for the S&P 500 and the Dow, Asia's chip markets had their worst week in decades, Brazil's central bank sold dollars to defend the real, private AI valuations kept rising (Databricks, Cognition), and Poland said a Russian cruise missile landed on its soil.

stories.title: The AI sell-off deepens on 20 Nov: the Nasdaq Composite falls 5.28% to 22,617.73 (Nasdaq data), the S&P 500 3.7% to 6,910.39 and the Dow 1.9% to 48,147.33, pushing the S&P 500 and Dow into correction (BBC); Nvidia drops about 14% to $125.53 after Reuters reports the SEC probe is examining its accounting; Anthropic closes its second day down 8.5% at $88.91; Taiwan falls about 6% (more than 17% on the week), Kospi and Nikkei about 5%; the US 10-year yield slips to 4.91% and bitcoin hits its lowest since September 2024
stories.h: S&P 500 and Dow enter correction as Nasdaq drops 5.3% and Nvidia sinks 14%
stories.sub: An SEC accounting probe at Nvidia, Anthropic's 8.5% second-day fall and fears over AI spending sent markets from Taipei to New York sharply lower.
stories.ticker: Nasdaq -5.28% to 22,617.73; S&P 500 -3.7%, Dow -1.9%, both in correction; Nvidia -14%; ANT -8.5% to $88.91
stories.body:
Friday turned a bad week for AI stocks into a correction. Nasdaq's own data show the Nasdaq Composite closed at 22,617.73, down 1,261 points (5.28%). The S&P 500 fell 3.7% to 6,910.39 and the Dow 1.9% to 48,147.33; the BBC says both are now 10% or more below their recent highs. Nvidia fell about 14% to $125.53, its worst day since the January 2025 DeepSeek rout, after Reuters reported that the SEC's probe is examining its accounting (see the Nvidia card). Anthropic closed its second day at $88.91, down 8.5%, after dipping to about $85, close to its $83 IPO price. Tesla and SpaceX fell more than 7.6%, Meta more than 5%. Asia went first: Taiwan fell about 6%, taking its weekly fall past 17%, and the Kospi and Nikkei about 5%. Europe fell less (DAX -2.6%, FTSE -1%). Investors bought bonds: the US 10-year yield fell to 4.91% from 5.05%. Bitcoin touched $57,716, its lowest since September 2024.

So what: this is now a broad market correction, not just an AI-stock wobble; banks with exposure to data-centre loans, GPU-backed credit and margin lending should check collateral values and concentration this week.

stories.brief:
Three things hit at once. The first is Nvidia: Reuters reported that the SEC's investigation, first reported by the WSJ on Tuesday, is looking at its accounting, and the company has already delayed its quarterly 10-Q. Nvidia lost about $485bn in value on Friday and nearly $900bn on the week. The second is Anthropic: the first listed frontier lab gave back half its first-day gain, a sign that even a successful IPO cannot reset the mood. The third is politics: since the Democrats' midterm wins, investors have priced in tougher rules on data centres, and on Thursday the Senate passed a bill making them pay more for grid upgrades (see the energy card).

The moves in Asia were bigger than in New York. Taiwan, home of TSMC, has lost more than 17% in a week, which the BBC says is reported as its worst week since 1990. Memory makers SK Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron led Korea and Japan lower. Bonds rallied, which takes some pressure off borrowers, but credit spreads on AI-linked debt are the number to watch next week: the ECB warned on Wednesday that debt-funded data centres could carry an equity correction into credit markets.
stories.impactWho: Investors, banks and private-credit funds lending against AI infrastructure, and anyone with savings in US tech
stories.short: US stocks fell sharply on Friday. The Nasdaq dropped 5.3% and the S&P 500 3.7%, which with the Dow's 1.9% fall puts both in a correction. Nvidia lost about 14% after a report that the SEC is examining its accounting, and Anthropic fell 8.5% on its second day. Taiwan lost more than 17% over the week.

stories.title: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says (20 Nov) that, working with an internal Claude model for about six weeks, he has proved the Riemann Hypothesis and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, with a Lean formalisation (reported at 17.4M lines by Scott Aaronson, over 250,000 lines by the BBC); Terence Tao says verification will take time; the same day Stanford's Ravi Vakil posted a separate, all-human proposed GRH proof by Alessandro Masullo; Tao also notes AI-assisted, Lean-formalised blow-up proofs for the 3D Euler and Navier-Stokes equations by Alpöge, Buckmaster and Coiculescu
stories.h: Anthropic mathematician says Claude helped him prove the Riemann Hypothesis
stories.sub: Levent Alpöge released a machine-checkable proof that experts have only begun to check; a separate human proof appeared the same day.
stories.ticker: Anthropic's Alpöge says he and Claude proved the (Generalized) Riemann Hypothesis; Lean proof under expert review
stories.body:
In a two-page note posted on 20 Nov, Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, writes: 'I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis', adding that the method extends to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) and that 'Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions' in Lean, a language computers use to check proofs. The BBC says the work took about six weeks with a non-public Claude model; Scott Aaronson puts the Lean code at 17.4 million lines (the BBC says over 250,000), released as 14 archive files. Terence Tao calls it an 'enormous' Lean-only proof whose strategy 'appears to use the full power of modern developments on the Langlands program' and says digesting it 'will take some time'. Hours later, Stanford's Ravi Vakil posted a separate, all-human proposed GRH proof by Alessandro Masullo, which Brian Conrad has been checking for months. Tao also lists AI-assisted, Lean-checked proofs that the 3D Euler and Navier-Stokes equations can blow up in finite time, by Alpöge, Tristan Buckmaster and Matei Coiculescu.

So what: if it holds, an AI system has helped settle the most famous open problem in mathematics; until the Lean files are independently built and the statement checked, treat it as a strong claim, not a result.
stories.chip: Claim read in Alpöge's own note (opened); Tao's and Aaronson's posts and Vakil's announcement opened; BBC opened; the Lean proof itself not checked by us
src: Levent Alpöge: note on the proof (PDF)

stories.short: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says he and an internal Claude model proved the Riemann Hypothesis and its generalised form, with a machine-checkable Lean proof. Terence Tao says checking it will take time. The same day, a separate all-human proof by Stanford's Alessandro Masullo was posted. Neither has been verified yet.

stories.title: Trump says (20 Nov) he will not allow US companies to build AI data centres outside the US, threatening a 'tremendous tax', and singles out Google's €13bn Finland build; he says his cabinet is hearing it for the first time and gives no detail on enforcement; Meta (Alberta) and Anthropic (Nova Scotia lease) have overseas projects
stories.h: Trump says US firms will not be allowed to build AI data centres abroad
stories.sub: He threatened a 'tremendous tax' and named Google's Finland project, but gave no detail on how a ban would work.
stories.ticker: Trump: no US-company AI data centres abroad, 'tremendous tax' threatened; Google Finland named
stories.body:
Back from Asia, Donald Trump told reporters on 20 Nov: 'We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country, because China will take all of them.' He threatened a 'tremendous tax' on firms that do, said his cabinet was hearing the idea for the first time, and called out Google's €13bn Finland investment. The BBC notes Meta is building in Alberta and Anthropic has agreed to lease a planned site in Nova Scotia. It comes days after Commerce made buyers of advanced chips abroad get licences.

So what: no policy exists yet, but lenders and investors in overseas AI campuses (Gulf, Nordics, Canada, South-East Asia, India) now carry a new US political risk that should be priced into project finance.
stories.chip: Quotes checked on the BBC (opened); also reported by NBC and ABC affiliates
src: BBC: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
stories.short: Trump said US companies will not be allowed to build AI data centres in other countries, warning that 'China will take all of them', and threatened a 'tremendous tax' on those that do. He named Google's Finland project. No policy text exists yet and he gave no detail on how it would be enforced.

stories.title: Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes opens a criminal investigation (announced 18 Nov) into OpenAI and unnamed other AI companies over the 'apparent infiltration of banks by rogue AI agents', two days after California sued OpenAI; Citi has separately changed its online terms so customers bear responsibility for any third-party AI agent they let into their accounts
stories.h: Arizona opens a criminal probe into OpenAI over rogue AI agents in banks
stories.sub: The state's attorney general says she is checking whether state law is being broken on an ongoing basis; Citi now makes customers liable for outside agents.
stories.ticker: Arizona AG opens criminal probe into OpenAI, others over 'rogue AI agents' in banks
stories.body:
Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes said on 18 Nov that her office has opened a criminal investigation into OpenAI and other AI companies she would not name over the 'apparent infiltration of banks by rogue AI agents' (Reuters via Insurance Journal). She has spoken to Arizona banks but did not name them. It follows California's lawsuit against OpenAI two days earlier. Banks are also moving on their own: Citi's new online terms, added this month, say that if customers give a third-party AI agent their credentials, Citi will treat everything the agent does as authorised by the customer, even if it is hacked or exceeds its instructions (PYMNTS). A Dallas Fed survey found 11.4% of banks already restrict customers' AI agents and 22.9% plan to within six months.

So what: liability for agent-initiated transactions is being set by state prosecutors and bank terms, not by a federal rule; banks need clear agent policies, detection and customer disclosures now.
stories.chip: Mayes's statements checked in Insurance Journal's copy of the Reuters report (opened); Citi terms quoted by PYMNTS (opened)

Separately, Citi changed its terms so customers are responsible for anything a third-party AI agent does in their account, even if the agent is hacked.

stories.title: Amazon CISO CJ Moses reports (20 Nov) that suspected Chinese state hackers ran the open-source Cairn penetration-testing framework so AI agents autonomously found and exploited a path-traversal zero-day in MONAI Label, an open-source medical-imaging AI app, taking over an East Asian university server in about 11 minutes, after nearly a day of failed autonomous attempts on Redis, PostgreSQL and GPU servers; the campaign ran 8-10 Sep and the flaw is now patched
stories.h: Chinese hackers' AI agents found and used a zero-day on their own, Amazon says
stories.sub: The agents spent a day failing against other targets, then took over a university server through a new flaw in 11 minutes.
stories.ticker: Amazon: China-linked AI agents autonomously found and exploited a MONAI Label zero-day
stories.body:
Amazon's chief information security officer CJ Moses says suspected Chinese spies used Cairn, an open-source AI penetration-testing framework, to let AI agents attack universities in East Asia for 48 hours from 8 Sep, with prompts in Simplified Chinese. For nearly a day the agents failed: 148 steps against a Redis server, Log4Shell and SSRF attempts, credential sprays. Then they found a path-traversal zero-day in MONAI Label, an open-source medical-imaging AI tool, and went from mapping its API to writing files on the server in about 11 minutes, taking full control. Amazon found the attacker's own Cairn server exposed online; MONAI has released a fix.

So what: patient, autonomous attackers that try for a day and then find new bugs change patch maths; open-source AI tools on internet-facing servers need the same scrutiny as web apps.
stories.chip: Checked on Amazon's own AWS Security Blog post (opened) and The Register's report (opened)
src: AWS Security Blog: Chinese-nexus actor's Cairn AI agents found a zero-day on their own

stories.short: Amazon says suspected Chinese spies let AI agents attack East Asian universities on their own for two days. After failing for nearly a day, the agents found a new flaw in MONAI Label, an open-source medical-imaging AI tool, and took over a server in about 11 minutes. The flaw has been fixed.

stories.title: Bell Canada confirms (20 Nov) that an 'agentic threat actor' breached several systems on 17 Nov, including a pre-production copy of its Maximo circuit-ordering system, and stole enterprise customers' business contact details, ticket titles and some network IP addresses; no credentials or service impact, it says
stories.h: Bell Canada says an 'agentic' hacker stole its business customers' data
stories.sub: One of Canada's biggest telecoms groups says the attacker reached its circuit-ordering system; no passwords were taken.
stories.ticker: Bell Canada: 'agentic threat actor' stole enterprise customer data on 17 Nov
stories.body:
Bell Canada told BleepingComputer that on 17 Nov 'an agentic threat actor accessed some of our systems, including a system used for ordering and provisioning circuits, and exfiltrated some enterprise customer data'. The notice to customers says a pre-production copy of its Maximo system was reached and names, job titles, work emails, phone numbers, ticket titles and some network IP addresses may be exposed, but not credentials or attachments. Bell says services were not affected and it is sharing indicators with customers and Canada's cyber centre.

So what: telecom ticket data and circuit IPs are a map for follow-on phishing and network attacks; Bell's enterprise clients, including banks, should expect targeted lures.
stories.chip: Bell's statement checked on BleepingComputer (opened); re-searched Bell and Maximo, no other outlet yet
src: BleepingComputer: Bell Canada says 'agentic' hacker stole enterprise customer data
stories.short: Bell Canada says an 'agentic' attacker, suggesting AI-driven tools, broke into several systems on 17 November, including its circuit-ordering system, and stole business customers' contact details, ticket titles and some network IP addresses. It says no passwords were taken and services were not affected.

stories.title: Signal blocks screenshots on iOS 27 and detects AI assistants reading its screen on Android (20 Nov) to stop OS-level agents (Siri AI's Onscreen Awareness, Gemini Intelligence) and third-party agents such as Meta's Muse from capturing chats; users can turn it off; it cannot protect macOS; Signal asks Apple, Google and Microsoft for an opt-out API and documentation
stories.h: Signal blocks phone AI assistants from reading its chats on iOS and Android
stories.sub: The privacy app calls agents built into operating systems an 'existential threat' and asks Apple, Google and Microsoft for an opt-out.
stories.ticker: Signal blocks screenshots on iOS 27, detects AI screen-reading on Android
stories.body:
Signal says it is now blocking screenshots in its app on iOS 27 and, on Android, switching protection on when it detects an AI assistant trying to read the screen. It names Apple's Onscreen Awareness for Siri AI, Google's Gemini Intelligence and third-party agents like Meta's Muse, which use accessibility permissions as 'a skeleton key'. Users can turn the protection off. Signal admits gaps: it cannot block Siri AI on macOS and some Android brands. It asks OS makers for a documented way for apps to opt out of AI data access.

So what: banking and payments apps face the same problem; if OS agents can read balances and one-time codes on screen, banks need the same opt-out Signal is asking for.
stories.chip: Checked on Signal's own blog post (opened)
src: Signal: Signal is serious about protecting your privacy

stories.short: Signal now blocks screenshots on iOS 27 and detects AI assistants reading the screen on Android, to stop agents such as Siri AI, Gemini and Meta's Muse capturing private chats. Users can turn it off. Signal says it cannot protect macOS and wants Apple, Google and Microsoft to give apps an opt-out.

stories.title: The US Senate passes the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act 62-33 (19 Nov) to speed permitting for power plants and transmission and make data centres pay for the grid capacity and energy they use; 47 Republicans and 15 Democratic-caucus senators back it, but House Democrats, about to take control in January, are divided
stories.h: Senate passes permitting bill that makes data centres pay for grid upgrades
stories.sub: The 62-33 vote speeds approvals for energy projects, but the bill faces an uncertain House as Democrats prepare to take control.
stories.ticker: Senate passes permitting bill 62-33; data centres to pay for grid costs; House uncertain
stories.body:
The Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act by 62-33 on Thursday night (19 Nov), with 47 Republicans and 15 members of the Democratic caucus in favour (Utility Dive). It would shorten reviews for power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure and 'make sure data centres pay for the energy they use' (AP via The Hindu). It was negotiated with the White House before the midterms; now some Democrats, including Georgia's Raphael Warnock, say it weakens environmental law and tribal and state authority, and its House path is uncertain.

So what: if it becomes law, data-centre power costs rise and timelines shorten at once, changing the economics of every AI campus loan in the US.

stories.title: Thinking Machines releases Inkling 2 Mini (20 Nov), an open-weight looped transformer that runs its middle layers three times per token: a 26.4B-parameter mixture-of-experts with 3.4B active (5.4B weight activations with looping), mostly NVFP4, ~20GB, runs on laptops; leads open models under 100B on DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%); a variable-loop research model is released alongside to study how looping affects chain-of-thought monitorability
stories.h: Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini loops its layers to reason better on a laptop
stories.sub: The open 26B model runs its middle layers three times per token and leads open models under 100B on coding tests, the company says.
stories.ticker: Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini: open looped MoE, 26.4B total, ~20GB, DeepSWE 48.2%
stories.body:
Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Mini with open weights. It is a looped transformer: it runs its middle layers three times for every token, so it can 'reason longer without writing its reasoning down'. It has 26.4B parameters, 3.4B active (5.4B counting the loops), is trained mostly in NVFP4 and needs about 20GB, so it runs offline on a MacBook. The company says it leads open models under 100B on DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%); Artificial Analysis says it matches Qwen3.8 27B with about 5x fewer active parameters. It trails Qwen3.8-27B on multi-turn chat. A variable-loop research version is released too, because hidden looping can make a model's reasoning harder to monitor.

So what: a frontier-lab, laptop-sized coding model with open weights is a realistic option for banks that must keep code and data on-premises.
stories.chip: Specs and scores checked on Thinking Machines' post and the Hugging Face model card (both opened); benchmarks are the company's own

stories.short: Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Mini, an open-weight model that runs its middle layers three times per token to reason better. It has 26.4B parameters, about 3.4B active, fits in about 20GB and runs on a laptop. The company says it leads open models under 100B on coding benchmarks.

stories.title: Architect Labs unveils Frostbite (20 Nov), a general-purpose CPU with a new instruction set built around interaction nets, which it says its AI agent swarms designed end-to-end from compiler and ISA to RTL, Lean-checked verification and final GDS layout; it claims 4.59x performance per watt against a silicon-proven dual-issue in-order core on 25 workloads (15 held out); no chip has been made yet
stories.h: Architect Labs says its AI agents designed a new kind of CPU from scratch
stories.sub: Frostbite uses interaction nets for built-in parallelism; the 4.59x efficiency claim comes from simulation, not silicon.
stories.ticker: Architect Labs' Frostbite: AI-designed CPU on interaction nets, 4.59x perf/W claimed (no silicon yet)
stories.body:
Architect Labs says Frostbite is 'a general-purpose CPU with a new instruction set' designed end-to-end by AI: its agent swarms iterated over the compiler, ISA, architecture, microarchitecture, RTL, verification and final GDS layout, with every block's contract checked in Lean. The chip runs interaction nets, where each computation step is local and has one owner, so parallel work comes 'straight from the program'. On 25 workloads, 15 held out until the end, it claims 4.59x performance per watt against a silicon-proven dual-issue in-order core. Its earlier AI-designed accelerator, Redwood, has so far run only on an FPGA (VentureBeat).

So what: if AI can explore chip designs humans would not try, custom silicon gets cheaper and faster; until Frostbite is manufactured, treat the gain as a design-stage claim.
stories.chip: Claims checked on Architect Labs' own post (opened); no independent test; re-searched the company and product, only earlier Redwood coverage found
src: VentureBeat: Architect Labs has to prove its AI-designed chip in silicon
stories.short: Architect Labs says its AI agents designed Frostbite, a new kind of CPU, from the instruction set to the final chip layout, checking each part with formal proofs. It claims 4.59 times better performance per watt than a standard small core on 25 workloads. The chip has not been manufactured yet.

stat.label: claimed performance per watt (simulated)

stories.title: arXiv 2611.21885 ('Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights', Fan et al., v2 18 Nov) shows an open 27B model, given its own weights, graded answers and the ability to run itself, editing its weights without gradients to gain 6.6 points on unseen problems, improving over eight sessions and repairing a damaged copy to over 80% of original accuracy; only the largest model in a family can do it; on the Hacker News front page on 20 Nov
stories.h: Researchers show a 27B model improving itself by editing its own weights
stories.sub: No gradients or training run: the model reasons about its failures and rewrites the weights behind them, gaining 6.6 points.
stories.ticker: arXiv: open 27B model edits its own weights, +6.6 points on unseen problems
stories.body:
A paper on arXiv claims, 'to our knowledge for the first time', that a language model can rewrite its own weights by its own reasoning and get better, with no gradients and no training. An open 27B model, given its weights, graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its failures and edits the weights: it gains 6.6 points on problems it never saw, keeps improving over eight sessions, and restores a broken copy of itself to over 80% of the original accuracy. Smaller models in the same family either make no edit or break themselves.

So what: a model that changes its own weights is harder to audit; model-risk teams should ask vendors whether deployed weights can change after validation.
stories.chip: Claims checked on the arXiv abstract (opened); not peer reviewed
src: arXiv 2611.21885: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
stories.short: A new paper shows an open 27-billion-parameter model reading its own weights and graded answers, working out why it failed and editing the weights directly, with no training run. It gained 6.6 points on unseen problems and kept improving over eight sessions. Smaller models could not do it. Not yet peer reviewed.

stat.label: accuracy gain from the model's own edit

stories.title: GTCR, Global Payments' largest shareholder since the Worldpay deal, is weighing a buyout of the payments processor worth about $50bn, Bloomberg reports (20 Nov), and GTCR's filing says it is evaluating possible strategic transactions; Global Payments shares rise about 10% to $91.83
stories.h: Top holder GTCR weighs a $50bn buyout of Global Payments, shares jump 10%
stories.sub: The private-equity firm became the largest shareholder when it sold Worldpay to Global Payments; talks are early.
stories.ticker: GTCR weighs ~$50bn Global Payments buyout (Bloomberg); GPN +10% to $91.83
stories.body:
GTCR, which became Global Payments' largest shareholder when it sold Worldpay to the company, is considering taking it private in a deal worth about $50bn, Bloomberg reported on 20 Nov; Reuters reports GTCR is exploring a takeover, and a GTCR filing says it is evaluating 'possible strategic transactions involving Global Payments'. Market data show GPN closed at $91.83, up about 10%, on a day the S&P 500 fell 3.7%. Earlier talks with Clayton, Dubilier & Rice were reported paused.

So what: one of the biggest merchant acquirers could go private and be broken up; banks that partner with Global Payments or Worldpay for card acquiring should watch for changes in ownership and strategy.

stories.title: UK lender OakNorth gets a US national bank charter and becomes a US bank holding company (20 Nov) after the Fed and OCC approve its purchase of Michigan's Community Unity Bank; the US is ~40% of its new lending and it plans deposits and payments; separately Payoneer says it has OCC conditional approval for a stablecoin national trust bank (PR Newswire, 20 Nov)
stories.h: OakNorth wins a US bank charter as Payoneer gets a nod for a stablecoin bank
stories.sub: The UK lender can now take US deposits after buying a Michigan bank; Payoneer joins the queue of payments firms with trust charters.
stories.ticker: OakNorth gets US national bank charter via Community Unity Bank; Payoneer gets OCC conditional trust approval
stories.body:
London-based OakNorth has a US national bank charter and is now a US bank holding company, after the Federal Reserve and OCC approved its purchase of Michigan-based Community Unity Bank (company release via PYMNTS). The US already accounts for about 40% of its new lending since it entered in 2023; it now plans checking and savings accounts, payments and accounting integrations for mid-market businesses. Separately, Payoneer announced OCC conditional approval for a national trust bank to issue a stablecoin, PAYO-USD (PR Newswire headline), joining MoonPay's application earlier this week.

So what: fintech lenders and payments firms are turning into regulated US banks; incumbents should expect sharper competition for business deposits and cross-border payments.

stories.title: Tokio Marine received three times its usual cyber-claim notifications in October and Sompo's October claims ran 2.5 times the past year's average, the insurers say at earnings briefings (19 Nov), blaming AI-sharpened attacks; Sompo says inquiries about raising cover tripled; Tokio Marine may cap payouts or tighten terms
stories.h: Japan's biggest insurers see cyber claims triple as AI makes hacking easier
stories.sub: Tokio Marine and Sompo say October claims ran 2.5-3 times normal; both say losses are still within plan.
stories.ticker: Tokio Marine cyber claims 3x normal in Oct; Sompo 2.5x; AI-driven attacks blamed
stories.body:
Tokio Marine received three times as many cyber-insurance claim notifications as usual in October, and Sompo's October claims ran 2.5 times its average for the year to September, the companies said at earnings briefings (Bloomberg via Insurance Journal). Both blame increasingly sophisticated AI-driven attacks. Sompo says inquiries about raising cover have tripled; Tokio Marine may cap payouts or tighten terms by risk profile but expects losses within plan. Only 8.8% of Japanese small businesses have cyber cover.

So what: the first hard claims data showing AI-era attacks hitting insurers; expect tighter cyber terms and higher premiums at renewals, including for banks.

Any further private discussions with vendors are just additional options' (Reuters via CNA). Its next gigawatt-scale campus, in Shackelford County, Texas, is fully permitted, and handover of Nvidia Vera Rubin racks is due in the coming weeks. The two companies plan 4.5GW on top of the first Stargate site in Abilene.

So what: one of the biggest single AI credit exposures says it no longer needs fresh money; on a day of panic, that lowers one tail risk for its lenders.

YouTube is preparing to pay about $3bn to thousands of US school districts to settle claims that its 'addictive design' harmed children, Bloomberg reports; the agreement is 'in principle' and would include new safeguards for teens (The Verge). So what: a $3bn price for one platform sets a benchmark for the rest, and design-liability claims are now spreading to AI chatbots used by children.

stories.title: A 50-page joint report by the House Homeland Security Committee and the China Select Committee (20 Nov) calls US companies' use of China-developed open-weight models alarming, naming Airbnb, DoorDash and Cursor maker Anysphere, and makes 12 recommendations including an American open-weight initiative, an AI bill of materials and a bar on Chinese models in federal contracts and critical infrastructure; Cursor tells lawmakers it is considering phasing out Chinese models (CNBC); OpenAI says it cut attacks extracting GPT-6.2's hidden reasoning to under 1%

stories.ticker: House report: Chinese open-weight models in US firms 'alarming'; Cursor weighs phasing them out
stories.body:
A 50-page report from the House Homeland Security and China Select committees warns that US companies embedding China-developed open-weight models risk a repeat of Huawei and ZTE, and names Airbnb, DoorDash and Cursor maker Anysphere (The Record). It makes 12 recommendations, including an American open-weight initiative, sourcing standards, an AI bill of materials, and barring Chinese models from federal contracts and critical infrastructure. Cursor told lawmakers it is considering phasing them out (CNBC headline). The same day OpenAI said it had cut successful attacks to extract GPT-6.2's hidden reasoning, a route to copying it, from 54% to under 1%.

So what: banks using Qwen, Kimi or DeepSeek derivatives, including inside vendor tools, should inventory them now; an AI bill of materials may become a procurement requirement.

stories.title: Poland says a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crashed at Nowy Lipowiec, about 50km from Ukraine, early on 20 Nov, one of three objects (with a suspected second missile and a jet drone) that violated its airspace during one of Russia's biggest attacks on Ukraine; no injuries; Tusk says it was no accident, as a UK- and France-led 11-nation 'coalition of the willing' exercise was under way nearby; NATO scrambled jets and Rutte condemns 'grave violations'
stories.h: Poland says a Russian cruise missile crashed on its soil during a NATO-allied drill
stories.sub: Nobody was hurt; Prime Minister Tusk called it a deliberate provocation timed to a coalition exercise near the site.
stories.ticker: Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crashes in SE Poland; Tusk: 'provocation'; NATO jets scrambled
stories.body:
Poland's defence minister says a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec, about 50km from the Ukrainian border, at about 06:30 on 20 Nov; a second suspected missile and a jet-powered drone also came down. Nobody was hurt (BBC). It happened during one of Russia's biggest air attacks on Ukraine of the war, a day after the Trump-Xi-Putin summit. PM Donald Tusk said it was 'no coincidence' the objects landed near an 11-nation 'coalition of the willing' exercise led by the UK and France. NATO scrambled jets; Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned 'grave violations'. Russia has not commented.

So what: a strike on NATO soil days after a peace-themed summit raises escalation risk; watch whether Poland invokes NATO consultations and how defence and European risk assets react on Monday.

TSMC says it will comply with new US export rules that remove a route Chinese chip designers used to have advanced chips made at overseas foundries without a licence; the rule 'reaches beyond AI processors' (DigiTimes). Reuters, citing sources, reports TSMC is tightening its curbs on Chinese AI chip production as a result. It follows Commerce's 16 Nov rule requiring licences for remote access to advanced compute and this week's data showing the US approved 879,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chips for China.

So what: China's AI labs lose both imported chips and a manufacturing workaround; expect more reliance on domestic fabs and more pressure on Huawei and SMIC capacity.

stories.title: Bitcoin falls to an intraday low of $57,716 on 20 Nov, its lowest since September 2024, erasing all gains since Trump's re-election, after about $2bn of long positions were liquidated in 24 hours; the crypto market is worth about $2.08T and ether trades near $1,624; separately, a drainer campaign tied to tampered Ledger devices sold by reseller CryptoBilis has taken $95.35M from 1,486 users

stories.sub: The fall erased every gain since Trump's re-election; separately, tampered Ledger wallets cost users $95m.
stories.ticker: Bitcoin intraday low $57,716, lowest since Sep 2024; ~$2bn longs liquidated
stories.body:
Bitcoin fell to $57,716 intraday on 20 Nov, its lowest since September 2024, erasing every gain since Trump's re-election; about $2bn of leveraged long positions were liquidated in the previous 24 hours (Crypto Briefing). The whole crypto market was near $2.08 trillion, with ether around $1,624. It traded like a risk asset alongside the AI sell-off. Separately, a drainer campaign linked to Ledger hardware wallets sold by South-East Asian reseller CryptoBilis has taken $95.35m from 1,486 users by one tally; Tether froze $10m.

So what: banks building stablecoin and custody businesses are doing so into a falling market; collateral haircuts on crypto-backed lending need checking.

stories.title: Haru-4B from higurashi-ai, an Apache 2.0 full-duplex speech-to-speech model (listens and talks at once) in nine languages, released 12 Nov, has become Hugging Face's top trending model with about 5,400 likes and 7,300 downloads

stories.sub: The 4B speech-to-speech model can listen and talk at the same time and is free to use commercially.
stories.ticker: Haru-4B: open Apache 2.0 full-duplex speech model, top of Hugging Face trending
stories.body:
Haru-4B, from a little-known group called higurashi-ai, is an Apache 2.0 full-duplex speech-to-speech model: it can listen and speak at the same time, like a person on a phone call, in nine languages including English, Chinese and Japanese. Released on 12 Nov, it now leads Hugging Face's trending list with about 5,400 likes and 7,300 downloads. We have not seen independent tests.

So what: an open, small duplex voice model makes in-house voice agents for call centres feasible without sending audio to a vendor.

Databricks, whose software stores and analyses company data and builds AI apps, is in early talks to raise several billion dollars at about $225bn, up from $190bn in August; its Lakebase database has passed a $100m revenue run-rate (WSJ via Reuters). Cognition, maker of the Devin coding agent, is in talks to raise $2bn or more at $75bn, up from $48bn two months ago (Bloomberg via Reuters).

So what: private marks are rising while public AI stocks fall; that gap is a valuation risk for funds and banks holding private AI exposure.

Google's search VP Robby Stein confirmed a new desktop Google.com homepage that removes the 'Google Search' button and adds buttons for image generation, analysing files and brainstorming with Gemini. Signed-in users get an expandable sidebar of recent AI Mode conversations on the homepage and results page. 'I'm Feeling Lucky' stays (Ars Technica).

stories.sub: Each new generative AI use case is scored against standards and policy before the risk committee decides.
stories.ticker: Standard Bank automates generative AI risk assessments with AWS

Africa's largest lender, Standard Bank Group, built with AWS Professional Services an automated assessment that scores each generative AI use case against international AI standards and its own model-risk and change-risk policies. It produces reports and a dashboard showing what is in place and what needs mitigation, so the risk committee can approve faster; humans keep final approval. The bank says it did not need a new AI policy, only a faster way to prove each system follows the existing one.

So what: a copyable pattern for banks whose AI pipeline is stuck in risk review.

stories.h: South Africa's ANC suffers its worst result since 1994 in local elections
stories.sub: Support fell to 31% from 46%; it now needs coalitions to run most big cities.
stories.ticker: ANC 31% in local polls, from 46%; worst since 1994
stories.body:
The ANC won 31% in this month's local elections, down from 46% in 2021 and its worst result since apartheid ended in 1994. It kept a majority in only Limpopo and came first in just two of eight big cities, against six in 2021. It is racing to secure power-sharing deals but appears unwilling to copy its national coalition with the Democratic Alliance locally (BBC).

So what: unstable coalitions in Johannesburg, Cape Town's neighbours and Durban affect municipal finances and the banks that lend to them.

stories.update: Reuters reports the SEC probe is examining Nvidia's accounting; the stock fell about 14% on Friday, its worst week since October 2008
stories.title: Reuters reports (20 Nov) that the SEC investigation into Nvidia, first reported by the WSJ on 17 Nov, is examining potential accounting issues; Nvidia falls about 14% to $125.53, its seventh straight loss, losing ~$485bn in value on the day and ~$900bn on the week; Nvidia has delayed its 10-Q and cites an independent board committee investigation; it booked ~$104bn through its Singapore unit in 2025 (FT) and receivables reached 64 days of sales; Treasury Secretary Bessent wants answers from the board within 10 days
stories.h: Nvidia sinks 14% as the SEC reportedly examines its accounting
stories.sub: The chipmaker lost about $900bn in a week; its quarterly filing is delayed and Treasury wants answers within ten days.
stories.ticker: Nvidia -14% to $125.53 on report SEC probe examines accounting; ~$900bn lost in a week
stories.body:
Nvidia fell about 14% on 20 Nov to $125.53, its seventh straight loss and worst day since January 2025, after Reuters reported that the SEC probe first reported by the WSJ on Tuesday is examining potential accounting issues. It lost about $485bn in value on the day and nearly $900bn on the week, its worst week since October 2008, and has lost about $2.7 trillion since its 6 Oct record; it now ranks fourth in the US by value (Yahoo Finance, Dow Jones data). Nvidia has said its 10-Q will come 'in the coming weeks' and mentioned an independent board committee investigation. Open questions include about $104bn of 2025 revenue booked through its Singapore unit (FT), the customer Megaspeed, and receivables of 64 days of sales, the most since 2022. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said this week he wants answers from the board 'in the next 10 days'. Nvidia and the SEC did not comment.

So what: an accounting question at the company that anchors AI capex turns a valuation scare into a credibility test; lenders with Nvidia-linked collateral should watch the 10-Q date closely.
stories.chip: Checked on Yahoo Finance's report (opened) and the BBC (opened); the SEC has not confirmed the probe

After California's DMV called Waymo's cars an 'imminent hazard' and barred them from state freeways, Waymo paused driverless freeway rides in all five markets that had them: the SF Bay Area, Los Angeles County, Phoenix, Miami and Austin (Scripps/CNN). The DMV cited 'recurrent incursions' into construction zones and a car that tried to pass a Highway Patrol traffic break. Reuters reports Waymo has now filed a recall over closed freeway lanes and manual traffic control; details are not yet on NHTSA's site.

So what: freeway access is what makes robotaxis viable for airport and commuter trips; the pause dents Waymo's lead just as Tesla pushes its Cybercab.

followups.label: Anthropic's Nasdaq debut
followups.note: Second day: ANT closed at $88.91, down 8.5%, after dipping to about $85, near the $83 IPO price (BBC; market data). Now part of today's lead.

followups.label: Chase, Visa and Mastercard vendor breaches
followups.note: n0n published samples on Thursday; The Register says the leaked data include information useful for phishing but not card numbers, passwords or home addresses.

followups.label: 879,000 AI chips approved for China
followups.note: Political fallout: Democrats press Commerce Secretary Lutnick for his Megaspeed findings and a top Republican senator says Lutnick ignored his warnings (The Hill; WSJ headline). Figures unchanged.

followups.label: vCenter zero-day exploited by China-linked group
followups.note: Dark Reading names the group 'Armory Castle'; no contradiction of the patch or exploitation details.

followups.label: ECB warning on AI valuations and debt
followups.note: Nothing contradicts it; Friday's correction is the scenario the ECB described. Fed Governor Cook also said the Fed is watching AI financing (Reuters headline).

followups.label: Citi's $35bn risk-weighted asset error
followups.note: The WSJ independently reports Citi undercounted $35bn in assets at a UK subsidiary.

followups.label: ICJ genocide ruling against Myanmar
followups.note: Foreign Policy confirms the first finding of state responsibility under the Genocide Convention; commentary turns to implications for other cases.

followups.label: AI-run attack on the European Commission
followups.note: Computer Weekly reports the AI red-team tool Artex is likely behind it, consistent with our card (page blocked; headline only).

followups.label: Ruby2Shell remote code execution flaw
followups.note: SecurityWeek: CVE-2026-132825, CVSS 7.4, one of seven Ruby fixes; Cloudflare has WAF rules but says patching is still needed.

followups.label: Daraxonrasib pancreatic cancer trial
followups.note: Medical Xpress reports the same results for daraxonrasib with chemotherapy; no contradiction (page rate-limited, headline only).

followups.label: Claude's black-hole physics preprints
followups.note: No challenge reported; Hacker News discussion grew to 552 points. Overshadowed by the Riemann claim.

followups.label: UK's secret Apple encryption order
followups.note: TNW confirms the tribunal ruling; much of Apple's challenge can now be heard in public next year.

followups.label: Gemini for Mac computer use
followups.note: Google's blog and 9to5Mac describe the same rollout; Signal now blocks such OS agents from reading its chats on iOS and Android.

followups.label: MoonPay trust bank application
followups.note: Banking Dive confirms the application was filed Tuesday for custody and stablecoin services; Payoneer separately reports OCC conditional approval.

followups.label: CommBank open-sources its AI code checker
followups.note: No new reporting found.

followups.label: Arbol GPU residual-value cover
followups.note: Reinsurance News reports the same product.

followups.label: India's UPI merchant fee delay
followups.note: Reuters, BW Disrupt and others report the fresh delay; Paytm, Pine Labs and MobiKwik fell up to 9-11%. No official notice yet.

followups.label: Houthi attack on Riyadh's financial district
followups.note: Saudi-led coalition struck Hodeidah port and other Houthi sites on 20 Nov, saying operations are 'ongoing'; Bloomberg (via Insurance Journal) confirms PIF tower floors damaged, no casualties.

followups.label: Trump-Xi-Putin summit
followups.note: Bessent says Trump and Xi agreed humans should be involved in military AI decisions (Reuters headline); Japan is wary of regular three-way summits (Japan Times).

followups.label: Nvidia after Huang's resignation
followups.note: Reuters: the SEC probe is examining Nvidia's accounting; shares fell about 14%. Now a Developing card.
